title: Recording short calls and emails as billable time on Mac, step by step for lawyers
metaTitle: Recording short calls and emails as billable time on Mac
description: Short calls and emails often go unbilled. Learn how to record them as billable time on Mac, with habits and fixes that cost nothing.
targetKeyword: recording short calls and emails as billable time
secondaryKeywords: log phone calls as billable time on Mac
time tracking for lawyers on Mac
intro: Short calls and emails often go missing from lawyer time entries. To record them as billable time on a Mac, log each one soon after it happens, in one place, with a matter number and a clear description. Then sweep your sent mail once a day. The research we checked does not measure this exact gap, so these steps focus on habits you can change this week.
tldr: Log each short call or email soon after it ends, with a matter number and a plain description.
Use a calendar block for calls and one tag or flag for emails, so both leave a trace on your Mac.
Run a daily sweep of sent mail and label anything you rebuilt from memory as estimated.
Paid tools like Timing can capture activity automatically, but check whether they track email before you pay.
Lazur can dictate, draft and point at things. It does not enter time for you.

blocks.text: Why short calls and emails go missing

Short calls and emails are small enough to skip. The problem is rarely laziness. Your day moves from one task to the next, and nothing marks the end of a call. An email reply feels like part of work you already did, so the time never gets a line of its own.

Some lawyers also choose not to bill certain short items on purpose. That is a valid choice when the firm allows it. The trouble starts when a choice gets made by accident. Thomson Reuters Institute notes that many partner write-downs are deliberate, so the gap between a choice and a miss matters.
A worked example from one ordinary day

Take a typical day. In the morning, a client calls about a deadline. Late morning, opposing counsel's office emails a scheduling request. Early afternoon, you send a reply from your phone. By late afternoon, you open the time sheet and recall only the longest discussion.

rows: Morning call with a client about a deadline
Calendar block plus one line in your time note
Email request from opposing counsel's office
Tag on the message, then an entry before the sweep
Flag it, then log it at the sweep
Logged with the time you guessed at the start
Log the actual time and the topic
blocks.caption: One ordinary day, and where short items usually get lost.

blocks.text: Read the table as a checklist, not a verdict. Each row shows one missing habit. Fixing one habit recovers the items it covers. You do not need all four changes on the first day.
Set up one capture point for calls

items: Open Apple Calendar and press ⌘N to create an event at the time the call started.
Title the event with the matter number first, then the purpose, such as call about lease terms.
Set the event length to match the call, even if the call was brief.
Add a one-line entry to your time note before you close the event.

blocks.text: A calendar block does two jobs. It shows the call on your day view, and it gives you a search target later. Search your calendar for a matter number to see every call on that matter. A call with no block shows up as a gap in the day.
Make email leave a trace

Email needs a tag, not a calendar block. In Outlook for Mac, select the message and look for Categorize on the Home tab. Choose one category named To log. In Apple Mail, use the flag button in the message toolbar. For Outlook steps in more detail, see [Outlook for lawyers on Mac](/for/lawyers/outlook).

blocks.title: Use one tag, not several
blocks.text: One flag or category works better than several. Two colors leave two piles to check, and the second pile is where items get lost.

For Apple Mail, the [Apple Mail assistant page](/apps/apple-mail) covers what Lazur can explain on screen. Neither step needs a paid tool. A tag only works if you clear it, so treat clearing as the last step of every entry.
Writing entries a client will accept

A good description says who, what and why in plain words. Call tells the client nothing. Call with client about lease terms, confirmed closing timeline tells them what they paid for. Keep it short, but keep the subject.

items: Matter number first, in the format your firm uses.
The action word: call, email, review or reply.
The subject in plain words, with no detail beyond what the matter needs.
The time, rounded the way your billing guidelines say.
The word estimated if you rebuilt the entry from memory.

blocks.title: Follow your firm's rules on client data
blocks.text: Entries often get copied into invoices and client portals. Follow your employer's rules on what client information may appear in a description. If you are unsure, ask your billing contact before you type it.
Edge cases that trip people up

items: Internal calls about a matter may or may not be billable. Check the rule before you skip them.
A call that turns into a meeting should be logged once, for the full time.
Emails copied to you with no reply may be reading time. Log them only if your firm bills for review.
Group emails covering several matters need one entry per matter, so the time lands on the right file.
Personal calls made on a work phone stay off the matter, even if they sit in the same log.

blocks.text: Each edge case passes one test. Would a client pay for this work on this matter? If yes, log it. If the answer is unclear, ask your billing contact and write down the answer for next time.
Mistakes that keep the gap open

items: Waiting for a perfect description. A rough line written today beats a polished one never written.
Logging only the calls you remember at the end of the week, then assuming the rest did not happen.
Using one catch-all entry like emails for a whole morning of work.
Keeping time on a sticky note or paper pad, then losing it before the sweep.
Changing an entry after it reaches a client without a note in your own log explaining why.

blocks.text: Paid tools that capture time automatically

If you want automatic capture, Timing is one Mac option. Its article for lawyers says it tracks apps, documents, websites, calls, meetings and calendar events. It assigns entries with rules and tags them Billable, Not Billable, Billed or Paid. The article does not name email, so test whether your mail app appears before you pay.

blocks.caption: Plans as listed on Timing's pricing page.

blocks.text: Annual plans are not pro-rated on refund, according to Timing's pricing page. Read that before you pay for a year. A third-party blog listed a different Professional price, so trust the pricing page.
Where Lazur helps, and where it stops

Lazur fits the typing and looking-up parts of this problem. Hold fn and speak an entry into any field. Ask Lazur to draft a one-line description from the email on screen. Ask where a button sits in Outlook or Apple Calendar, and Lazur circles it. You still read the entry, check the matter number and save it.

Lazur does not click buttons, enter time or run your billing system. It only looks at your screen while you hold the shortcut. Think of it as help with typing and finding things, not a time tracker. Lazur has a 3-day Pro trial with no credit card. Check [pricing](/pricing) before you decide.
Catching up on an existing backlog

If the gap already exists, start with the most recent stretch. Older work is harder to rebuild, and a rough rebuild is still a record. Use the Sent folder and your calendar as guides. Mark every rebuilt entry as estimated, and tell your billing contact how you handled it.

Do not bill from a rough rebuild without checking it against something real. Each entry should point to a sent message or a calendar event. If nothing points to it, leave it out of the bill and keep a note of it.

faq.question: Should I log every short call?
faq.answer: Log any call that moves a matter forward. Then decide with your billing contact what goes on the invoice. Writing it down keeps the choice yours. Skipping it quietly removes the choice.

faq.question: Is a short email billable time?
faq.answer: It can be, depending on what the email did and your firm's rules. A reply that gives advice on a matter is more likely to count than a receipt. Check the billing guidelines before you decide.

faq.question: How do I bill a call that lasted less than a minute?
faq.answer: Check your firm's minimum increment. Some firms round up to a minimum unit. Others leave very short items off the bill. Ask billing which rule applies, then follow it on every item.

faq.question: Can Lazur enter the time for me?
faq.answer: No. Lazur can dictate the text, draft a description and point at the field. You check the matter number and save the entry yourself. Lazur does not click buttons for you.

faq.question: What if I already missed weeks of entries?
faq.answer: Rebuild from your Sent folder and calendar, mark the entries as estimated, and tell your billing contact what you did. Do not invent detail the records do not support.

faq.question: Does Timing capture email?
faq.answer: Timing's article for lawyers does not name email specifically. Test whether it records your mail app before you pay. Its pricing page lists plans by Mac count and user count.

faq.question: Do I need to buy anything to fix this?
faq.answer: No. A time note, a calendar block, one tag and a daily sweep cover most of the problem. A paid tool helps if you want automatic capture across apps.

faq.question: Does this apply to nurses or accountants too?
faq.answer: The habits carry over, but the rules differ. Follow your employer's rules on client or patient data, and check your own billing or time-keeping guidelines before you start.

problem: short calls and emails left off time entries

costs.title: Money that never reaches an invoice
costs.text: Thomson Reuters Institute research says the average law firm partner writes down about 300 hours a year of their own time. Many of those write-downs are choices, not forgotten work. Forgotten entries are a separate problem, and the public research does not split the two. A short call that never becomes an entry is still work the client never sees.

costs.title: A thin billable day
costs.text: Clio's 2017 Legal Trends data, as reported by National Jurist, found lawyers bill about 2.3 hours of an 8-hour workday. After realization and collection, about 1.6 hours are collected. Administrative tasks account for 48% of the average day. Short calls and emails sit inside that admin share. The article does not measure how much of it goes unrecorded, so treat the gap as a warning, not a figure to subtract from your bill.

costs.title: Long days that get longer
costs.text: A 2016 national survey of attorneys found 28% reported depression symptoms at a mild level or higher, using the DASS-21 scale. The study's authors say long hours and minimal sleep are likely to add to that distress, especially in the first 15 years of practice. The study does not examine time entries. Still, rebuilding a week of calls late at night adds work to a day that already runs long.

costs.title: Vague entries invite questions
costs.text: A client who sees entries that say only call or email may ask what the time bought. Specific entries show the work. Vague entries also give a reviewer a reason to cut the time. Clear descriptions protect the work you already did, and they make a review faster for everyone.

causes.title: Short tasks feel too small to log
causes.text: A short call feels like nothing, so it never earns a place in your head. Lawyers track the big items, such as the draft, the hearing or the deposition. Small items drop out. The fix is to log by habit, not by how important the task feels.

causes.title: A call has no natural end point
causes.text: A document has a save button. A call ends, and you move straight to the next task with no pause. Email arrives in a stream, so each reply looks like a small break, not billable work. Without a marker, the time has no edges and no record.

causes.title: Phone calls happen away from the Mac
causes.text: Many calls happen on a desk phone or a mobile phone, away from the computer where your time system sits. Nothing on your screen shows that the call happened. Without a calendar block or a note, the call leaves no trace until you try to remember it.

causes.title: The time system lives in another app
causes.text: Email sits in Outlook or Apple Mail. Your time entry may sit in a separate practice tool. Switching costs attention, so the entry waits. Waiting turns into forgetting. Keep the capture point close to the email, not in a separate place you open once a week.

causes.title: Entries wait until the end of the week
causes.text: Small details fade quickly for most people. A call from Monday is harder to describe on Friday, so the entry gets shorter, vaguer or skipped. Reconstructed entries are also easier to undercount. The fix is timing, not a better memory. Log the item while the details are fresh.

causes.title: Minimum increments are unclear
causes.text: If your billing guidelines set a minimum increment, a short call may still be worth a billable unit. Many people skip anything that feels too short without checking the rule. Ask your billing contact what the rule says for calls and emails. Then the decision is made once, not on every call.

causes.title: Replies sent from a phone
causes.text: You answer a client email on your phone between meetings. The reply goes out, and nothing records it. Replies sent on a phone are easy to miss, so plan a tag or flag for them before you leave the desk.

fixes.title: Keep one running time note
fixes.text: Open Apple Notes and create a single note titled Time. After each call or email, add one line with the date, the matter number, the action and the time spent. A rough line written today beats a polished entry never written. Use the same note every day, so there is one place to check.

fixes.title: Put every call on your calendar
fixes.text: In Apple Calendar, press ⌘N to create an event at the time the call started. Title it with the matter number and the purpose, such as call about lease terms. Set the length to match the call. Calendar events show on the day view, and you can search them later by matter number.

fixes.title: Tag emails as you handle them
fixes.text: In Outlook for Mac, select the message and look for Categorize on the Home tab. Choose one category named To log. In Apple Mail, use the flag button in the message toolbar. Use one tag only, so there is one pile to clear. Remove the tag after the entry is saved.

fixes.title: Run a daily sweep of sent mail
fixes.text: Pick one fixed time each day, such as before lunch or at 5 p.m. Open Sent in Outlook or Apple Mail. Search by each client's address in the To field. Compare each sent message with your time note. Add any missing lines before you close the laptop.

fixes.title: Build a mail rule for client addresses
fixes.text: In Apple Mail, open Mail > Settings > Rules and add a rule. Match the client's address in the From or To condition, then move the mail to a folder named To log. Test the rule on one client first. A narrow rule protects personal mail. A broad rule can hide real client mail, so check the folder each day.

fixes.title: Speak the entry with built-in dictation
fixes.text: Turn on Dictation in System Settings > Keyboard > Dictation. After a call, speak the entry into the time note. Say the matter number first, then the action and the time. Read the text back before you save it. Spoken notes are quick, and short entries suit speech well.

fixes.title: Ask billing a few questions once
fixes.text: Ask your billing contact a short list of questions. What is the minimum increment for short calls? Do administrative emails get entries at all? Write the answers in your time note. Then follow the rule on every short item, so you are not guessing each time.

fixes.title: Label anything you rebuilt
fixes.text: If you must rebuild a day from memory, say so in the description with the word estimated. Ask your firm how it wants estimates marked. Do not add detail the records do not support. A short, honest entry protects you more than a long guess, and it keeps the time record clean.

plan.label: Morning
plan.title: Set up your capture points
plan.text: Create the Time note in Apple Notes. Pick one tag for To log in Outlook or Apple Mail. Add a daily reminder for the mail sweep. This takes one sitting, and then the habit runs on its own.

plan.label: After calls
plan.title: Log one line before the next task
plan.text: Create a calendar event for any call that mattered. Then add the one-line entry to the Time note. Keep the line short. Add detail later only if you need it.

plan.label: After emails
plan.title: Tag now, log at the sweep
plan.text: Tag any email that needs an entry, using the one category or flag you chose. Do not open a second window to log it now. The tag keeps the item in view for the sweep.

plan.label: End of day
plan.title: Run the sweep
plan.text: Open Sent, search by each active client's address, and compare the results with the Time note. Add missing lines. Clear the tags on anything you have logged.

plan.label: Friday
plan.title: Clear the week
plan.text: Review the Time note and the To log folder. Mark rebuilt entries as estimated. Ask billing about any unclear increment, and write the answer down for next week.
